prologue.title: Now
prologue.subtitle: A machine shed, two hours of gravel from town

norway.title: Norway
norway.subtitle: A fjord in the west, about the year 870

knows_he_bled.description: Aud said the uncle left bleeding, and that somebody in the hall did it

hrapp_owes.description: You kept the smith alive in front of the hall

walter.name: Walter
walter.notes: Your uncle. The hall calls him Unkel, having taken the word for his name.

kol.name: Kol
kol.notes: A boy of about eleven, with a dog. He finds everything first and tells everyone.

thorgrim.name: Thorgrim Ketilsson
thorgrim.notes: The hersir. It is his hall, and his half pound of silver.

aud.name: Aud Ketilsdóttir
aud.notes: Thorgrim's sister. The keys are hers.

hrapp.name: Hrapp
hrapp.notes: The smith. He does your uncle's voice.

hild.name: Hild
hild.notes: Gyda's apprentice at the healing. She keeps a stick.

finn.name: Finn Ormsson
finn.notes: Orm's son. He builds by looking.

eyvind.name: Eyvind
eyvind.notes: A skald. He goes between the halls and says who is dead. Invented; not the Eyvind of the next century.

ulfar.name: Ulfar
ulfar.notes: Hrapp's brother, one farm up the water. His boy died at harvest.

welder.label: A welder
welder.description: You join steel for a living and have the forearms to prove it. You have never done it without electricity.

nurse.label: A nurse
nurse.description: Eleven years on a surgical ward, most of them nights. You know what a wound ought to look like on the third day.

teacher.label: A history teacher
teacher.description: You have explained the fall of Rome to fifteen-year-olds every spring for nine years. Nobody has asked you to prove any of it until now.

engineer.label: An engineer
engineer.description: You can say why a bridge stands up and what it will cost. Other people have always done the building.

rider.label: Rode as a child
rider.description: Every Saturday until you were sixteen. Somebody else always caught the horse, and somebody else fed it.

charm.label: Easy to like
charm.description: People tell you things. You have never been sure what you do to cause it, and have learned not to ask.

martial.label: Martial arts
martial.description: A brown belt, earned twice a week in a hall that smelled of feet. Nobody there was trying to kill you.

fencer.label: Fenced
fencer.description: Three years of foil, with a mask, a referee and a rule about whose turn it was.

speaker.label: Used to a room
speaker.description: You can stand up in front of two hundred people and be heard at the back. What you said when you got there has varied.

hunter.label: Hunts
hunter.description: A week every autumn, with a rifle and a flask, and the truck forty yards behind you.

sailor.label: Sails
sailor.description: Summers on a lake, in a boat that belonged to somebody's father. You know where the wind is before you know you have looked.

farm.label: Raised on a farm
farm.description: Chores before school for sixteen years. Animals have never frightened you, and have never impressed you either.

tall.label: Tall
tall.description: You have found most door frames the same way.

slight.label: Slight
slight.description: People hand you things to hold.

broad.label: Broad
broad.description: Strangers ask you to help them move house.

blunt.label: Blunt
blunt.description: You say it, and afterwards you find out whether you should have.

quiet.label: Quiet
quiet.description: You are often taken to be agreeing.

cheerful.label: Cheerful
cheerful.description: It has been held against you.

the_door.label: Through the stone
the_door.description: This is as far as the story goes: the whole of the Norway visit. Japan is next, and is not built yet. The four years can be tried here as a sandbox: their rules, with no story written.

n_hill.title: The hill
n_hill.text:
The rain finds you first. It comes in sideways, fine and cold, and the heather is up to your shins and soaking through your jeans before you have drawn a breath. The warmth of the shed is gone as if it had never been. Behind you there is no frame, no bench and no concrete floor, only a boulder the size of a grain truck, grey and streaming, with a seam of white quartz running down its face like a line of chalk.

Somebody has been at the quartz with a nail. Scratched into the white, at about the height of a short man's shoulder, are a letter and a row of marks.

::clue boulder_tally::

Nine of them. Counted again, there are still nine.

Then you turn around, and the whole country drops away at your feet.

The hill falls in grey rock and rust-red bracken, down and down, to water so dark and so still that the mountains stand in it upside down, every ledge and streak of snow doubled. It runs inland between walls of stone that climb straight up into the cloud and are lost there. Far across, a waterfall hangs on the rock like a thread of white wool, falling without a sound. No wire crosses the sky. No road is cut into the far shore. There is the rain hissing in the heather, and one bird calling somewhere below, and under those a quiet so wide that it seems to have weight.
[break]
On a shelf of green land at the water's edge stands a building. It is long, longer than the machine shed, and low, and its roofline bows gently from end to end like the keel of an upturned boat. Grass grows on the roof, as thick and green as a pasture. Smoke seeps out along the ridge with no chimney to guide it, and lies down flat in the rain. Smaller roofs cluster round it. Strips of field run down to the shore, pale with stubble, and on the shingle below them two boats have been hauled out side by side, long and lean, each one rising at the bow in a single clean curve.[if trait.sailor]

The wind is coming up the water from the sea, and the smoke agrees with you. Both boats lie with their sterns to it, set that way by hands that did not need to check.[/if]

There is one like them in a museum at home, behind glass, black as coal and cracked along every plank, held together with steel rods. These two are the colour of dark honey. Rain runs off them. A coil of rope lies in the nearer one where somebody dropped it this morning.

Your phone lights up at a touch: sixty-one per cent, no service, a photograph of your own kitchen. It goes back in your pocket.

The cold has got into your hands by now. In the lee of the boulder there are sticks, of a kind, and a clump of heather that pulls up easily, and your uncle's lighter makes a brave small flame that the wet heather swallows whole. Steam comes off it. The bark of a little twisted birch curls and blackens and goes out. The note comes out of your pocket, and is turned over once, and goes back. By the time the lighter is too hot to hold there is a thread of smoke, and a smell of singed grass, and nothing else.
[break]
"Hvat ertu?"

A boy stands a few yards up the slope with a dog at his knee and a stick in his hand. He is ten or eleven, bare-headed in the rain, and his clothes are the exact brown-grey of the hillside, which must be how he has come so close. The dog is rough-coated and yellow-eyed, and has already made up its mind.

Behind your ear the brass thing clicks, twice, like a relay closing.

"What are you?" the boy says again, and now the words come in English, half a beat behind the movement of his mouth, like a film with the sound slipped. What, he has said. Not who.

[if manner == blunt]"Cold," you tell him.[elif manner == quiet]You hold up both hands, which have gone the grey of the boulder, and let them answer for you.[elif manner == cheerful]"Cold, thanks," you tell him, as if he had asked at a bus stop.[else]"Lighting a fire," you tell him, across the small wet heap that is not one.[/if]

[if manner == quiet]He frowns, and looks from your hands to your face.[else]The words leave your mouth in a shape you did not give them, and the boy frowns, as people do at a thick accent.[/if] His eyes go to the sticks, and then to the lighter, a moment before your hand closes over it.

He crouches. From the pouch at his belt he takes a curl of steel, a flake of grey stone and a pinch of something black and soft as felt. With his back to the wind and one knee on the heap of sticks he strikes once, twice, and blows, and there is a flame. He feeds it with shreds of birch bark drawn from inside his shirt, dry and warm from his own skin. He does all of it by feel. His eyes have not left your jacket.
[break]
"Can I?" he says, and has the tab of the zip between finger and thumb before the words are out. He draws it down. The teeth part. He draws it up, and they knit together again behind it, and his mouth opens a little. Down, and up. Down, and up. The fire crackles and the rain ticks on your shoulders, and he does it eleven times.

"Unkel had one of these," he says at last. "On his trousers."

"You know my uncle?"

"Everyone knows Unkel." He says it as another boy might say that everyone knows the weather. "He owes Thorgrim a ship."

Then, finally, his eyes drop to what you are carrying.

[if kit == bag]The bag is open before you can move.

[if occupation == welder]The helmet goes onto his head and comes straight off again, since the world went dark inside it. He turns the gloves over and nods at the stitching. Then he finds the file. He tests its edge with his thumb, and draws it once along the back of his own fire-steel, and a bright curl of metal lifts away and drops into the heather. He looks for a long moment at the flat it has left.

"You are a smith," he says. "Hrapp is our smith." The file goes back into the bag a good deal more gently than it came out. "Hrapp is going to hate you."[elif occupation == nurse]The scissors please him. The gloves he blows up like bladders, knots, and offers to the dog, which backs away. Then he lifts out the stethoscope by one earpiece, studies it, and puts the wrong end in his mouth. You fit it to his ears and press the cold disc to his chest. He goes perfectly still. His lips move, counting. After a while he takes the disc and holds it against the dog's ribs and listens to that too, and looks from the dog to himself and back.

"You are a healer," he says. "Gyda is our healer." He hands the thing back by its tubing, at arm's length, as he might hand over a live eel. "Gyda is going to hate you."[elif occupation == teacher]Out come thirty-one essays on the causes of the First World War, already going soft in the rain. He turns the pages slowly, and then faster, and stops when he sees that the marks on one sheet are not the marks on the next, and that every page was made by a different hand. The red pen clicks under his thumb, in and out, in and out, until it is taken from him. He draws a line with it across the back of his hand and holds the hand out into the rain to see whether it will wash away. It does not.

"You make marks for remembering," he says. "Ulf remembers for us. He needs no marks." He gives the essays back in a wet stack, in no order at all. "Ulf is going to hate you."[else]The hard hat goes onto his head and stays there. The calculator he shakes beside his ear, in case something inside it is loose. Then he finds the tape measure. He draws out an arm's length of yellow steel, lets go, and jumps as it whips home. He does it again. Then he hooks the end over the dog's nose and walks the tape down its spine to the tail, and the dog stands for it with great dignity: forty-one inches.

"You measure things," he says. "Orm builds our ships, and he measures nothing. He looks." He feeds the tape back into its case by hand, an inch at a time, watching where it goes. "Orm is going to hate you."[/if]

He seems to be looking forward to it. His name is Kol, he says, and he swings the bag onto his own shoulder and sets off down the hill at a trot, shouting long before the yard can hear him that he has found something on the mountain, and that he found it first.[elif kit == notebook]It lies open on your knee, with the rain spotting the page. This is the page.

::clue notebook_people::

"You're Kol," you say.

The boy's hand stops on the dog's neck. "Who gave you my name?"

There is no answer he would like. You turn the book round and hold it out to him. He leans forward, not too far, and looks at the lines of capitals as he might look at the tracks of an animal he has only heard stories about. The rain taps on the paper. The last line on the page has been gone over and over, in blue ink and black ink and pencil, until the box round it has nearly cut through.

Kol goes down the hill ahead of you without once looking back, and he does not wait at the turns. By the time you come into the yard, a long while behind him, a surprising number of people have found work to do near the door of the hall, and they all straighten up at once.[else]He peers into it, and is not impressed. So you tear a corner from the bag of sugar and shake a little into his cupped palm, white on the wet skin. He looks at it, shrugs, and licks it up, plainly expecting salt.

Everything about him stops. Rain runs down his face. Very slowly he licks the palm again, all the way to the wrist, and then he leans over the sack to see how much more there is, and draws the neck of it closed with both hands, and ties it in a knot that would hold a bull.

"Do not give that to anybody on the way down," he says. "They will only want it."

His name is Kol. You may walk behind him. In the yard he tells a woman carrying two buckets, and after her the hens, that the stranger is his, that he found it, and that nobody is to touch the sack.[/if]

choices.text: Go down to the hall.

n_hall.title: Unkel's water
n_hall.text:
The path down is wet moss on wet rock, and your boots were made for a concrete floor. A good part of the hill goes by sitting down.[if trait.rider]

A horse stands in the yard, thick-necked and shaggy, no bigger than a large pony and the same dun as the hillside. It turns its head as you pass and looks you up and down exactly as the ponies at the riding school used to, and then it looks away.[/if]

The hall is bigger from the yard than it was from the hill, a long dark flank of timber under its green roof, and the door is low.[if looks == tall] It is lower than it looks. The lintel is oak, and very hard.[elif looks == broad] You turn your shoulders and go through it at a slant, like a sofa going up a staircase.[elif looks == slight] You pass under it without stooping, the only person all day to do so.[/if]

Inside there is no light at first, only warmth and the smell of smoke. Then the fire shows itself, a long trench of embers and flame running down the middle of the floor, and the dark draws back from it by degrees: benches along both walls, faces, the glint of a brooch, and rising from the floor on either side a double row of posts as thick as trees, because they are trees, each one whole. Every post is carved. Beasts climb them from the floor to as high as the firelight reaches, long-bodied things with gripping paws, each biting the next, knotted through one another so tightly that there is nowhere to lay a fingertip between them. The light slides over them as the fire shifts, and they seem to breathe. Above them the roof is lost in smoke. The air smells of wet dog and roast meat and wool, and of a great many people, [if looks == forgettable]none of whom has turned round. A man is telling his neighbour what he paid for a ewe. A woman laughs. It is a small child, in the end, who stops with a crust halfway to her mouth and points.[else]thirty or more, and they have all turned to look. The talk dies a bench at a time, from the door to the far end, until there is only the fire.[/if]
[break]
Close by the hearth a man sits with his sleeve pushed back and a cut laid open across the heel of his hand. An old woman holds him by the wrist. Beside them a girl is lifting a small iron pot off the embers with two sticks, the steam rolling off it.

"Eighteen," the girl is saying. "Nineteen. Twenty. That is four."

"That is three," says the man with the hand.

"It is four, Bjorn. I have my thumb on it."

"Then your thumb moved."

They count it again. On the last twenty the old woman tips the pot, and the water runs steaming over the cut, and the man lets his breath go through his teeth. She binds the hand with a strip of cloth fished out of the same pot, still too hot to hold.

"Unkel's water," Kol says at your elbow, in the voice of a boy explaining to somebody slow. "You boil it for a hundred. Nobody is going to count a hundred for a pot, so we count twenty, five times." He lifts his chin at the man. "Bjorn put an axe in his own leg last winter, and it should have come off. Unkel washed it in his water every day and shouted at anybody who touched it, and Bjorn still has the leg."

"Did he say why it works?"

"He said there are beasts in water, too small to see, and the boiling kills them." Kol looks up at you sideways, to see how you take that. "Nobody listened to that part. But the leg stayed on. So we boil it, and we leave out the beasts."
[break]
At the head of the fire stands the only seat in the hall with a back to it, and in it sits a man of fifty or so, with a grey-shot beard and forearms like the roots of the posts beside him. He has not moved since you came in. Now he lifts one finger from the arm of the chair, and the whole hall watches you walk the length of the fire to him.

[if kit == bag]"Kol tells me he has found something useful," Thorgrim says. "The last one off that hill told me he was useful as well."[elif kit == notebook]"Kol tells me you had his name before he gave it," Thorgrim says. "Have you mine?" You have, and you say it, and on the bench nearest you people shift a little further along.[else]The tin of pepper and a card of needles go down on the board in front of him. He prises the lid off the tin, bends to it, and sneezes like a horse, and comes up delighted. "Unkel came with his hands empty and went away with them full," Thorgrim says. "You have it the other way about."[/if]

"You are his kin, though. Anyone could see it. You have his clothes, and you stand in my hall as he did, as if you were waiting for somebody to explain it to you." Laughter runs along the benches. "He ate at my fire from hay-time until the leaves turned, and he ate well. He kept Bjorn's leg on, and reminded us of it most evenings. I liked him. He said he could build me a ship that would sail into the wind. I asked how, and he drew it in the ashes, and it was a handsome drawing. I gave him half a pound of silver to buy iron. Six nights ago he went up that hill with it, and he has not come down."

"What do you want with a ship that sails into the wind?"

Thorgrim looks into the fire for a moment before he answers. "There is a king working his way along this coast," he says, "and he has the wind behind him." He lifts his eyes. "Tonight you are my guest. Tomorrow you are Unkel's kin, and you have what Unkel owes. We will talk about my ship when you have eaten."
[break]
[if hero.sex == male]They give you the end of the bench nearest the door, where the draught comes in and the dogs lie, and where a stranger sits until the hall has decided about him.[else]They give you the end of the cross-bench at the far wall, where the women of the house sit, and six pairs of eyes go over you from your wet hair to your boots, a good deal more carefully than Thorgrim's did.[/if]

A girl comes with a basin of water and a cloth over her arm, and holds them out. The water steams a little. It has been a long day. You look at the basin, and at the girl, and in the end you wipe your hands down the legs of your jeans and nod to her, and somewhere along the bench somebody makes a small strangled noise.

A woman has stopped behind the girl. She is about your own age, in a dress of deep rust red, with her sleeves pushed back to the elbow from some work she has left half done, and from her belt hangs an iron ring of keys, a dozen at least, that chime when she shifts her weight. All along the bench people have drawn in their feet to let her by. She has watched the whole business with the basin. Not a muscle of her face has moved, and it is costing her something.

"Hands in the water," she says. "Then the cloth. Then you eat. Unkel had it by his second month."

The bowl, when it comes, is wooden and hot, with something grey in it and grains of barley floating in that. There is no spoon. Up and down the hall people are drawing their own out of belts and sleeves and pouches. She unhooks one from beside the keys, pale horn, worn as thin as a leaf along one edge, and holds it out. When your fingers close on it, hers do not let go.

"I have had this longer than I had my husband," she says. "I want it back."

That is Aud, Kol tells you, loudly enough for half the bench. Thorgrim's sister. The keys are hers, and so is everything they open.

choices.text: Eat.

n_choke.title: The smith's throat
n_choke.text:
Across the fire a man with burn-scarred forearms is telling his end of the bench a story, and he is doing a voice. It is a fussy, eager voice, a voice that explains things. It comes through the brass ear, across eleven hundred years, and it is your uncle Walter to the life: the little cough before each new point, the way a sentence climbs when he is sure of himself. The men around him are weeping with laughter. He gets as far as the ship, and stops.

Nobody notices at first. He has a mouthful, and a man with a mouthful may stop. But then he is on his feet, with one hand flat on the board and the other at his throat, and no sound is coming out of him at all. The man beside him laughs and thumps him between the shoulder blades. The smith's face is going dark, and then darker, the colour of a plum.

[if occupation == nurse]Your body is over the bench and round the end of the fire before the rest of you has caught up. Eleven times, on the ward, and twice for the same old man.[else]A church hall, years ago, on a wet afternoon: a rubber torso on a trestle table, and a patient man called Keith showing a dozen bored people where to put their hands. Your feet are already taking you round the fire.[/if]

Then you are behind him, with your arms round his middle and a fist under his ribs and the other hand locked over it, and you pull, hard, up and in.
[break]
Benches scrape. Three men are on their feet. One has a knife in his hand, the short one he was cutting his meat with, and he is coming round the end of the bench with it held low, because what the hall can see is a stranger with both arms round its smith from behind. You pull again. Something flies out of the smith's mouth and lands in the embers with a hiss.

He drags in a breath that sounds like a door being forced. Then another. Then he says something over his shoulder, hoarsely, and the brass ear clicks once and leaves it exactly as it was.

The hall has gone silent. The man with the knife has stopped where he stands, though the knife is still in his hand, and the firelight runs along it.

"What," says Thorgrim, "did you do to my smith?"

choices.text: Tell him it is a hold your people use for a bone in the throat.
Tell him the man was choking and now he is not, and sit down.
Tell him how it works.

n_hold.title: A hold
n_hold.text:
"It is a hold," you say. "Where I come from it is taught, for a bone in the throat. The fist goes here, under the ribs, and you pull up and in."

Thorgrim nods slowly. All along the benches shoulders come down. A hold is a thing this hall understands; they wrestle here all winter, when the snow has shut the door. The man with the knife slides it back into its sheath and comes closer, and asks to be shown where the fist goes.

You show him on Kol, who has put himself forward by standing nearest. Before the bowls are empty three pairs of boys are at it by the door, squeezing one another breathless, and one of them has been sick in the straw. The old woman who poured the water comes down the hall, wiping her hands, to ask what words are said with it. None, you tell her. Her face falls. Kol whispers that there will be words by morning all the same.
[break]
The bench goes quiet when Aud sits down on it beside you.

"'Where I come from it is taught,'" she says, and she has caught your voice nearly as well as the smith caught your uncle's. "That was well put. Unkel would have told us why it works, and Hrapp would have died listening."

"It is taught, where I come from."

"I do not doubt it." She lifts the horn spoon out of your bowl, turns it to the fire to see that it is whole, and hooks it back beside the keys. "Hrapp will not thank you. He hates to owe anybody, and he liked Unkel less than any of us did. I would keep out of the forge for a day or two."

choices.text: Find somewhere to sleep.

n_silent.title: Your barley
n_silent.text:
"He was choking," you say. "Now he isn't."

You step back over the bench and sit down. The bowl is where you left it, still warm, and the barley has swollen.

For a few breaths the only sound is the fire. Then the hall begins, a murmur at the far end that runs up the benches like flame along a twig, and it does your explaining for you while you eat. By the time the spoon scrapes wood you have been a wrestler from the east. You have been one of Unkel's people, who carry healing in their hands, as everybody knows. The old woman who poured the water is telling anyone who will listen that you squeezed something out of Hrapp that had been sitting in him since midwinter, and that he is the better for its going. Nobody asks you which of these it was. Thorgrim sends a boy to move you four places up the bench, into the warmth of the fire, and a stranger with a red beard leans across and fills your cup.
[break]
Aud comes for her spoon when the bowl is empty.

"You let them tell it," she says. "Unkel never once managed that. He would have been on his feet by now, drawing in the ashes."

"There wasn't much to tell."

"No." She takes your hand and turns it palm upward to the firelight, and reads it for a moment like a thing with writing on it. Then she gives it back. "I will want to hear it, all the same. It need not be tonight."

choices.text: Find somewhere to sleep.

n_explain.title: Two pipes
n_explain.text:
"There are two pipes in the throat," you say. "One is for air and the other is for food. The meat went down the one for air. There was still air in his chest, under the meat, so I squeezed the chest, and the air pushed it out."

Silence. Bjorn lifts his good hand and feels along his own neck. The old woman who poured the water asks, in the tone of somebody being very fair, why a man cannot then breathe and swallow at once, all day long. There is a flap, you tell her. It closes.

"A door," says a voice further down the bench. "In the throat."

"A small one."

The words hang in the smoke. Thorgrim looks at you from the head of the fire, and there is no unkindness in his face at all.

"Unkel talked like this," he says. "The beasts in the water."
[break]
Hrapp, who owes you the breath in his body, has moved one place further down the bench. Along both walls people are studying their bowls. Then there are fingers on your sleeve, and Aud is walking you the whole length of the hall, past all those lowered eyes, to the post beside the door, where she stops with her back to the room and the keys still swinging at her hip.

"Was it true? About the pipes."

"Yes."

"I thought it might be. Unkel's were mostly true as well." Behind her the talk is starting up again, low. She keeps her voice beneath it. "Listen. They will take a true thing out of your hands any day of the year. Out of your mouth it is only talk. The last one here who talked like that went up the hill six nights ago with his hand wrapped in his shirt."

"Whose knife was it?"

"Eat your barley," Aud says. "And I will have my spoon back when you have."

choices.text: Find somewhere to sleep.

n_night.title: The first night
n_night.text:
They bank the fire with turf for the night, and the hall goes to sleep around you all at once, as a barn does: a hundred small shiftings in the dark, a cough, a dog sighing, and then only breathing. Rain is falling on the grass overhead. It makes almost no sound, a hush like a hand drawn across cloth, and now and then a drop finds its way down through the smoke-hole and hisses on the embers.

[if kit == bag]The bag is under your head, with your hand through the strap.[elif kit == notebook]The notebook is inside your jacket, flat against your ribs.[else]Kol is asleep across the hall with the sack under him and one arm thrown over it.[/if] [if road.first == hold]By the door two boys are still practising the hold on each other, in whispers.[elif road.first == silent]Somewhere down the bench a man is still explaining you to his neighbour, and getting it wrong.[else]There is an arm's length of empty bench on either side of you.[/if]

In the morning you will be Unkel's kin. Somewhere above the turf and the rain, and eleven hundred years away, a yard light is still burning at noon.

choices.text: Sleep.

n_morning.title: Unkel's kin
n_morning.text:
A weight lands across your shins before it is light: one of the dogs, which has decided in the night that you are furniture.

Morning comes into the hall from above, a grey shaft of it falling through the smoke-hole, and people rise out of the dark and step over one another, yawning, scratching, hunting for shoes. Somebody is waking the fire with fresh birch. Nobody has forgotten last night. [if road.first == hold]Beside the hearth two small boys have a third locked in the hold, and the old woman who poured the water stands over them correcting the grip. She has a name for it now. Unkelstak, she calls it: Unkel's grip, though Unkel never laid a hand on anybody.[elif road.first == silent]Two women pass with their arms full of bedding, talking across you without lowering their voices, and from them it is plain that the stories were settled into one overnight. You are a healer who wrestles.[else]The bench is empty for an arm's length on either side of you, as it was last night. A small girl creeps up, looks hard at your throat, and is called sharply away.[/if]

Aud goes by with a stack of bowls and puts the top one into your hands without breaking stride. "Thorgrim is at the shore," she says over her shoulder. "He wants you to see what your kinsman left him. Eat first. You will want it in you."

Kol is in the doorway with the dog, wet with dew to the knees. He has been up the hill already, as he is every morning, and he has news: the wet smell by the white stone is fainter than it was yesterday. He reports it as he would report a lame ewe. Beyond him the rain has stopped, and the fjord lies under a lid of white mist, with the mountains standing out of it like islands.

choices.text: Go down to the shore.

n_keel.title: The ship that is not there
n_keel.text:
The boat shed stands open at both ends, like your uncle's, and the morning comes straight through it. It smells of pine tar and fresh-cut oak, and the floor is soft underfoot with years of shavings.[if hero.sex == female] Half the shed has been given over to a sail: a huge brown weight of wool laid across three trestles, with four women bent over it, their needles flashing. They look up all together, like one animal with eight eyes. There is an empty stool at the fourth trestle.[/if]

[if hero.sex == female]In the other half lies your uncle's ship.[else]And there in the middle of it lies your uncle's ship.[/if] There is a keel, as long as the hall is wide, with a stem curving up at one end and a stern at the other, and four planks rising on each side, overlapping like the feathers of a wing. After that there is nothing. The oak has silvered where the weather reached it. In the bow, on a bed of dry grass, a wagtail has built a nest.

"Orm laid it at midsummer," Thorgrim says. "Your kinsman stood where you are standing and told him where everything went. Orm has built ships since before I had a beard. He did as he was told as far as the fourth plank. Then he put down his axe, and said he would not lay another on a thing he could not see in his head." He nods toward a big grey man at the far end of the shed, who is fitting a rib and does not look round. "I have paid for the oak."

A wooden bowl sits upside down on a flat stone beside the keel. Thorgrim crouches and lifts it away with both hands, gently, like the lid from a dish.

::clue ash_drawing::

"Nobody has been allowed to sweep there," he says.
[break]
[if occupation == engineer]It is a dinghy. The lines in the ash are the lines every ten-year-old draws on the back of an exercise book: a triangle of sail set fore and aft, a mast, a hull like a slice of melon. He has given a ship of this size the rig of a holiday boat, and drawn nothing at all below the waterline to stop it sliding sideways. A thing built to that drawing would sail into the wind for exactly as long as it took to fall over.[elif occupation == welder]Whether it would sail is anybody's guess. But the mast in the drawing is stayed with four fittings, and he has taken trouble over them: his fingertip has gone back to square the shoulders of each one. Every one of them would need a lathe. He always did like a fitting.[elif occupation == nurse]A ship or a bathtub, it is all one to you. But the hand is unmistakable. He has drawn the wind as an arrow with a little barb at the tip, exactly as he draws arrows on the notes he leaves on his own fridge, and if ash would take lettering he would have labelled it.[else]That sail is in books. It belongs to boats from seas a long way south of here, lean boats with their canvas set along the hull instead of across it. Nobody on this coast has ever seen one, and by every account nobody on this coast will build one for a very long time to come. What he promised Thorgrim was not so much a ship as a different history.[/if]

Thorgrim sets the bowl back over the drawing. "Three days," he says, straightening. "Orm says the weather holds three days, and after that nothing is built until spring. You are his kin. Go where you can be of use, and at the noon meal tell me what kind of use it was."

His footsteps go away up the shingle. The wagtail comes back to the bow with something in its beak. From the forge across the yard comes the ring of a hammer, and from the south wall of the hall a thread of steam, where the cloths are boiling.

choices.text: Stay in the boat shed.
Go to where they boil the cloths.
Go to the forge.

n_boat.title: The fifth plank
n_boat.text:
A young man is lying under the keel with an adze, and long pale shavings are curling away from the blade and falling on his chest. He slides out when your shadow crosses him. He looks at your face, and then at your hands, as everyone here does.

"Finn," he says. "Orm's son. You are the other one."

"The other one."

"Unkel's. He stood where you are for a month and told my father how a ship is built." There is no heat in it. He brushes the shavings from his shirt. "My father has not been the same since. I thought it was the best month we ever had."

There is not a drawing in the shed, nor a rule, nor so much as a length of knotted string.[if occupation == engineer] The tape measure stays in your pocket.[/if] Finn takes up a plank and offers it to the one below, and shuts one eye, and looks along the seam with the other for the space of a breath. Then he takes the plank away and shaves off a sliver no thicker than a fingernail. When he offers it up again the two edges meet along their whole length, and the morning light that was showing between them goes out like a candle. On the door post beside him is a row of cuts, one for every plank that has gone on at the first try.

::clue finn_tally::
[break]
"You may hold that end," he says.[if hero.sex == female] At the trestles the needles stop.[/if]

The plank is green oak, split from the log along its own grain, heavy and cool and smelling like a cut apple. It is the fifth, the one his father would not lay, and Finn is laying it because nobody has told him not to. It has to take a twist as it comes round to the stem. He leans on it, and the wood creaks, and gives, and creaks again. Then it speaks: one flat crack, like a branch breaking. A split has opened at the edge beside the third rivet hole. It runs a finger's length toward the heart of the plank, pale and clean, and stops.

Finn says a word. The brass ear lets it through untouched.

[if occupation == welder]A crack travels because its tip is sharp. Take away the sharpness and it has nowhere to go: one hole, drilled just beyond the end. It worked on a stock trailer, and on a fuel tank, and one winter on the frame of your own truck, lying on cardboard in the snow.[elif occupation == engineer]A crack travels because its tip is sharp. Take away the sharpness and it has nowhere to go: one hole, drilled just beyond the end. There are four pages of yours in a filing cabinet somewhere recommending exactly that for a footbridge, and a man with a drill did it in a morning.[else]There was a garage once, and a crack creeping across a windscreen, and a man in overalls who put a tiny drill to the glass just beyond the end of it. The crack ran into the hole he had made and stopped dead, with nowhere sharp left to go. Forty dollars. It had looked like a conjuring trick.[/if]

choices.text: Tell him your people bore a hole at the end of a crack, to give it somewhere to stop.
choices.text_after:
"Where I come from, we bore a hole at the end of a crack," you say. "Just past it. It gives it somewhere to stop."

Finn looks at the split, and then at you, for a long moment. Then he reaches up for the auger himself. He sets the point a thumb's width beyond the end of the crack and turns it through, the shavings spiralling out, and when he puts his weight on the plank again the split creeps forward into the hole, and stays there.

"Somewhere to stop," he says, and then again, more slowly, trying the words out for his father before his father is there to hear them. By the time the rivets are clenched he has it worked out to his own satisfaction: the hole blinds the crack, so that it cannot see which way to run. He tells you this kindly, as a thing you may not have known.

choices.text: Take the auger off the wall and bore it.
choices.text_after:
The auger hangs on a peg by the door post. You take it down, set the point a thumb's width beyond the end of the crack, and turn it through, with the pale shavings spiralling out over your knuckles. Then you lean on the plank. The split creeps forward into the hole, and stays there.

Finn has watched every turn of it without a word. He drives the rivets. A while later, further along, a second plank begins to go with the same flat crack, and the auger is in his hands before you have straightened up. He bores the hole himself, a thumb's width beyond the end. He does not look round while he does it. The back of his neck has gone red.

choices.text: Tell him why a crack runs.
choices.text_after:
"It runs because the end of it is sharp," you say. "All the pull in the plank comes to that one point, and the point tears. Make the end round, and the pull is spread about, and there is nothing to tear."

Finn has gone very still. His lips move on the word. "Sharp," he says, and he lays his thumbnail against the tip of the crack as if it might cut him.

"Wood has no pull in it." Orm has not turned round. His voice comes down the length of the shed like a plank being dropped. "It has grain. Bore your hole." Somebody laughs. Finn bores the hole. The split creeps into it and stops, and in all the shed his is the only face that changes.

n_bench.title: Hild's stick
n_bench.text:
Against the south wall of the hall, out of the wind, a fire burns under an iron pot, and the steam goes up white into the morning. The old woman from last night is feeding it with split birch. Beside her a younger woman is lifting strips of linen out of the boil on a forked stick and laying them along a rail to dry, where they smoke gently in the sun.

The old woman is Gyda. She looks at you once, as one cat looks at another across a yard.

The younger is called Hild. She is perhaps twenty, with a burn-scar on one wrist and her hair tied back in a rag, and thrust through her belt, where another woman would carry a distaff, is a stick.

::clue hild_stick::

"This edge is the ones we washed with the boiled water," she says, running her thumb along it. "That edge is the ones we did not, before he came. A cut for every wound. A cross-cut through it if the wound went bad." She turns the stick in the light. One edge is crowded with crosses. The other has two. "Gyda says it was the weather. I think weather would be on both edges."

[if occupation == nurse]Three days of lectures, a textbook as thick as a brick and an examination went into teaching you what she has done here with a knife and a stick.[else]Somewhere far ahead of this morning there are men in wigs, and hospitals full of the dead, and several centuries of argument, before anybody thinks to do what she has done here with a knife and a stick.[/if]

"Nobody asked you to keep that," Gyda says, without looking up from the fire.

"No," says Hild.
[break]
A woman is coming across the yard with a child in her arms. He is three years old, perhaps, and he lies against her shoulder without holding on. Two days of fever, she says, and the flux with it; and this morning he stopped crying, and she was glad. His lips are cracked. His eyes have sunk back into their sockets, and the skin of his arm, when Gyda pinches it, stays pinched. Gyda presses his belly and calls for ale with an egg beaten into it.

[if occupation == nurse]The fever is not what is killing him. He is drying out, and there is perhaps a day in it. Water, with salt and something sweet, a spoonful at a time from now until dark: most of them come back.[else]It is printed on the back of a packet in every chemist's shop at home, with a little drawing of a spoon: water, salt, something sweet, a little at a time, all day. It is never the fever that takes them. They dry out.[/if]

choices.text: Tell them it is your grandmother's cure.
choices.text_after:
"My grandmother had a cure for this," you say. "Boiled water, honey, and a pinch of salt. A spoon at a time, for as long as he'll take it."

Gyda has given honey for the flux for forty years, and says so, at some length. Salt she does not hold with. But a grandmother is an authority she understands, being one, and after a moment she jerks her chin at Hild, and Hild mixes the cup. The child's mouth opens for the first spoon like a bird's. Then for the second. The sun climbs the wall. By noon half the cup is gone, and the mother has slid down with her back against the warm stones and her eyes shut.

"Whose grandmother?" Hild says, very low, with the knife already moving on the stick. She has begun a third edge.

choices.text: Mix it, and start spooning.
choices.text_after:
There is a cup on the bench. You fill it from the pot of boiled water, stir in a thumb of honey from Gyda's own crock and a pinch from the salt box, and sit down on the ground beside the child with the horn spoon from last night. Nobody stops you. Gyda's hand comes halfway up, and goes down again.

His mouth opens for the first spoon like a bird's. Then for the second. The sun climbs the wall. By noon half the cup is gone. Gyda has watched every spoonful go in, with her arms folded, and when the mother asks her in a whisper what the stranger is giving him she says, "Honey," which is a third of the truth, and the third she can stand behind.

Hild's knife is moving on the stick. She has begun a third edge.

choices.text: Tell Hild what is happening inside him.
choices.text_after:
You say it to Hild, because she is the one with the stick. "It isn't the fever that kills them. Everything is running out of him, and he's drying up. The water puts it back. The salt makes the water stay, and the honey gets the salt in."

She does not look at you as the hall did last night. Her eyes go to the child's cracked lips, and to the cup, and back, measuring one against the other. "Drying," she says slowly. "Like fish."

"Like fish," says Gyda, and her voice carries to the far side of the yard. "He says your boy is drying like a fish." The mother's arms tighten, and she turns the child away against her own body. So it is Hild who mixes the cup, and Hild who kneels and spoons it, a little at a time, exactly as it was said. By noon half of it is gone. The stones of the wall are warm against your back, where you have been standing all morning.

n_forge.title: The bellows
n_forge.text:
[if hero.sex == female]Aud is crossing the yard with a basket on her hip, and she changes direction without slowing. Something cold and heavy is pressed into your hand: a long iron key with its bit snapped off. "Hrapp can mend that," she says, "and you can wait while he does." Then she is gone, and there is a reason for you to be standing at the door of the forge.

[/if]The forge sits by itself at the edge of the yard, well away from anything that might catch, a low stone hut with a roof of turf and a doorway black with soot. Heat comes out of it like breath. Inside, Hrapp is at the anvil with a bar of iron glowing orange in the tongs, and he does not stop for you. The hammer rises and falls. His voice, when it comes, is a rasp. He swallows, and winces, and his eyes flick to you and away.

"I am alive," he says to the iron. "I had noticed. You need not have come to see."

A boy works the bellows in the corner, about Kol's size and a great deal quieter. Something is wrong with them. Each stroke ends in a wheeze, and the coals brighten only on every second one, so that he is pumping twice for each breath the fire draws, with the sweat running off his chin.

"Your kinsman mended those," Hrapp says. The hammer comes down. "They were not broken." It comes down again. "He put a tongue of leather inside, so that the air would go one way only, and for a month they blew like the north wind, and he told me about it daily. Now the tongue sticks." He turns the bar in the coals. "I have kept a count of what he owes this forge."

::clue hrapp_marks::

The first cut is the sign that begins your uncle's name, the boy says, barely moving his lips. The rest are days.
[break]
[if occupation == welder]There have been a great many bellows through your shop. The sound of this one tells the whole story: leather gone dry, curled at the edge, catching on the rim of its own hole. Out, a palmful of fat worked into it, one stitch at the hinge, back in. A quarter of an afternoon.[else]Down on one knee beside the bellows, with your cheek almost on the wood, there is a hole to look through, and inside the throat a flap of leather hanging from a hinge. It has dried and curled like a dead leaf, and at each stroke its edge catches on the rim. The cat flap in your own back door does exactly this every winter. Fat, and a stitch at the hinge.[/if]

choices.text: Tell him your people grease the tongue at every new moon.
choices.text_after:
"At home we grease the tongue at every new moon," you say. "Then it never dries."

"Every new moon." Hrapp lets the hammer rest on the anvil. It is the kind of thing a man can do something with; anybody can remember a moon. He sends the boy running for tallow. The leather comes out as stiff as bark and goes back supple, with a stitch at its hinge, and at the first stroke the bellows draw one long clean breath and the coals go from orange to white.

Hrapp stands looking at them. "He never said anything about the moon," he says, and he sounds almost cheated.

choices.text: Take it out, grease it, and put it back.
choices.text_after:
The peg comes out of the throat of the bellows with a twist. The leather behind it is as stiff as bark. You hold out an open hand toward the boy and wait, and after a moment he understands, and comes back at a run with a lump of tallow. The fat goes in under your thumbs until the leather bends like a glove. A stitch at the hinge, with an awl from Hrapp's own bench. The peg goes home. At the first stroke the bellows draw one long clean breath, and the coals go from orange to white.

Hrapp looks at the fire. Then he looks at you. "He would have talked through the whole of that," he says. The boy's mouth falls open. It may be the kindest thing that has ever been said in that forge.

choices.text: Tell him why it sticks.
choices.text_after:
"It sticks because the leather has dried," you say. "When it dries it curls, and the curl catches the edge of the hole. The air is pushing it the right way. It just can't get past itself."

The hammer comes down on the anvil and stays there. It is the first time it has been still since you came in.

"He explained it too," Hrapp says. "He explained the bellows, and he explained the fire. And then one night he walked down the hall and explained to my brother why his boy was dead." His hand closes on the hammer again. "Grease it or leave it. Do not tell me about it."

So you grease it, in silence, with the boy holding the tallow. At the first stroke the bellows draw one long clean breath, and the coals go from orange to white, and the hammer begins again.

n_skald.title: The skald
n_skald.text:
At noon the food is cold, and people eat it wherever they happen to be standing. [if counter.place >= 3]A girl carries yours across the yard to you on a board, and two men by the wall watch her do it.[else]Yours is on a board inside the door, where the dogs have had to be spoken to about it.[/if] Thorgrim comes down from the high end with a rib of mutton in his fist, and wants to know what kind of use you were. [if road.day == boat]You held the end of a plank, you tell him. Finn, from further down the wall, says it was the right end.[elif road.day == bench]You fed a child with a spoon, you tell him. Gyda says, across you, that it was her honey.[else]His smith's bellows are blowing, you tell him. Hrapp, who has come up for his meat, says that this is so, and carries the meat away to eat it somewhere else.[/if]

That is when every dog in the yard stands up at once. A man is coming down off the hill path through the last of the mist, and he walks into the yard, and across it, and in at the door of the hall, as a man walks into his own house.

He is as lean as a rake, and wet to the thighs. He carries a staff, and he wears a broad hat, which he keeps on until everybody has had a good look at him in it. The hall's welcome is the welcome a pedlar gets: glad, and a little wary, because he has things they want and they will have to feed him for them.

"Eyvind," Kol says at your elbow. "He goes between the halls and says who is dead."
[break]
With a horn of ale in his hand and the steam rising off his cloak, Eyvind gives them the news. The king's ships are lying at the mouth of the next fjord but one. He counted eleven. From every farm they are taking a tenth of what it has, and the names of the men who work it. He lets that settle. Then he says that a verse came to him on the way over the hill, and would the hall care to have it, and the hall would.

His voice changes when he begins. It drops, and rings, and the lines come in pairs with a beat like oars. The brass ear clicks and stumbles and falls behind, and whole phrases arrive as nothing but noise. But enough comes through. There is a short man from the south, soft in the hands. He promises a great lord a ship that will outrun the wind. He eats the lord's mutton for a summer. He walks into a stone. All down the benches people are rocking with laughter and wiping their eyes, and the only still face in the hall is Thorgrim's.

When it is done he comes and folds himself onto the bench beside you, smelling of wet wool and the road.

"You are the kinsman," he says. "I will want something for the next hall. They will ask me what came after the short man." He turns the empty horn in his fingers. "What came after him?"

choices.text: Tell him the truth: a shed, a door, a letter.
choices.text_after:
So you tell him. A shed, two days' ride from any sea. A door standing in the middle of the floor with no wall round it. A letter. He does not interrupt once. When it is finished he sits looking at the fire, and his lips are moving.

"A door in a stone," he says at last. "With no house to it. A man goes in at one side and does not come out at the other." He is counting something off on his fingers. "Nobody will believe a word. It scans, though." He is already humming. Somewhere along this coast, for years to come, children are going to be asked it as a riddle.

choices.text: Give him something better.
choices.text_after:
You came by sea, you tell him. From a country so far to the south that the ships carry two masts. You are looking for a kinsman who wandered off. He nods along, and has begun improving it before you have finished. By the bottom of his next horn there are three ships. You left a great house to come. Your kinsman is a kind of holy fool, and your people are bound by an old law to fetch such men home.

"That one will travel," he says, and claps you on the knee, well pleased with both of you.

choices.text: Tell him to ask again when you have done something.
choices.text_after:
"Ask me again when I've done something," you say.

His eyebrows go up under the brim of the hat. "That is what the good ones say," he says. "Also the ones who never do anything." But a skald cannot walk out of a hall with a hole in his news, and by evening there is a verse regardless. In it you are tall, and silent. You came out of the stone at night. Nobody knows what you want. Kol has it by heart before supper, and is saying it to the hens.

n_counsel.title: The king's tenth
n_counsel.text:
Nobody brings out the gaming boards that evening. The fire is built up until the carved beasts on the posts seem to move, the small children are herded to the far end, and the hall talks about the king.

There are three things a hall can do, and by the time the first horn has gone round each of them has a bench to itself. Bjorn and the grey heads are for paying. A tenth is a tenth, and there have been winters that took more. The young men round Finn, Orm's son, are for the shore and their axes, since eleven ships is not so very many, and Thorgrim lets them say it twice before he asks, mildly, which of them has ever seen eleven ships. And then there is the third thing. It is said low, and mostly from the women's bench, and Hild, who helps Gyda with the cloths, says it loudest: that there is land in the west. A summer's sail beyond the islands. Grass to the knee, and rivers full of fish, and not one soul living on it. Eyvind, by the fire, has met a man who wintered there.

So that is what the ship is for. Not to fight in. To leave in, with the wind dead against him and the king behind.
[break]
[if hero.sex == female]It is Aud who asks you, on the cross-bench, low, while the men are shouting. "Your people live a long way off, and have seen more kings than we have. What do they do when one comes?" And when she has her answer she stands, and says it to the hall as a thing she has heard, and the hall listens to her as it would never have listened to a stranger.[else]"You," Thorgrim says, down the length of the fire, and the shouting stops. "Unkel's kin. Your people live a long way off, and have seen more kings than we have. What do they do when one comes?"[/if][if occupation == teacher]

There is a name for this king. There is a date for how long he lasts, and a paragraph in a book on your own shelf about what becomes of the people who sail west. All of it has been chalked on a board, on a wet Thursday afternoon, for thirty children who were looking out of the window. Every face in the hall is turned toward you now, waiting.[/if]

choices.text: Tell them to count it: the tenth against the ship.
choices.text_after:
"They count it," you say. "What the tenth costs you, every year, for as long as there is a king. What the ship costs you, once. Then they look at the two heaps."

It is a small thing to say. But it is the first thing anybody has said all evening that a person can do with their hands, and Bjorn is already sweeping a space clear on the bench and reaching for a pouch of gaming pebbles. One heap grows, and then another. Voices rise over whether sheep go in as sheep or as wool. And at the head of the fire Thorgrim has stopped looking into the flames, and is leaning forward with his elbows on his knees, looking at the heaps.

choices.text: Tell them the truth: kings like this one win.
choices.text_after:
"Kings like this one win," you say. "Where I come from there is always a king in the end. The halls that fought him are in songs. The ones that paid him are still there."

Nobody thanks you. Round Finn the young men's faces close like doors, as though somebody had spat on the floor. But Thorgrim nods, slowly, a man reading a bill he has been expecting for some time; and Aud says to nobody, to the fire, "And the ones that leave?"

"I don't know what becomes of the ones that leave," you say. [if occupation == teacher]In the book on your shelf it takes up most of a page.[else]The fire shifts and settles. Nobody else in the hall knows either.[/if]

choices.text: Ask who in the hall wants to go.
choices.text_after:
"Before they decide anything," you say, "they ask who wants to go."

Thorgrim looks at you, and then down the hall. "Well?" he says.

Nobody had asked. The silence goes on long enough for a log to burn through and fall. Then they begin to answer, one at a time, and it does not go by benches at all. Finn wants to go; his father, beside him, would sooner be buried under his own boat shed. The woman whose child had the fever wants to go, and says so with the child asleep in her lap. Gyda says she is too old to be seasick, and will pay the king in good advice. Aud says nothing. Thorgrim's eyes pass over her, and do not stop.

n_last_night.title: The well
n_last_night.text:
Late, when the fire has burned down to a red seam and the hall has drawn off into its corners, the rest of it comes out: what your uncle did on his last night here.

[if road.first == explain]Aud brings it. She comes down the dark hall with the keys held still in her fist, so that they will not ring, and sits where nobody else will, which is beside you. From the purse at her belt she takes a folded scrap of paper.

"He left the other half," she says. "It was under his bowl. I have not shown it to my brother."

::clue note_half::

"Hrapp has a brother. Ulfar. One farm up the water." Her voice is very low. "His boy died at harvest. A fever, and the flux, and three days. Your kinsman was fond of the boy. He sat up with him. And afterwards, when the ale was in, he went and told Ulfar why." She turns the paper over. There is nothing on the back. "Ulfar's well lies below his byre. He said the water had killed the boy. He was very sure, and very sorry, and he said it here, in front of everyone."

"What did Ulfar hear?"

"That his well was cursed. That Unkel had known it was, and watched." The embers tick. "It was Hrapp who got the knife off him." She puts the paper into your hand and closes your fingers over it. "Ulfar has not sat in this hall since."[elif road.first == hold]It is the boy from the forge who tells you. He slides onto the bench beside you in the dark, smelling of charcoal; anybody who can put Hrapp on the floor is worth knowing, it seems. He tells it in scraps, in a whisper, with his eyes going to the door between each one.

Hrapp has a brother, Ulfar, on the next farm up the water. Ulfar's boy died at harvest: a fever, the flux, three days. Unkel sat up with him. And afterwards, here in the hall, with the ale in him, Unkel stood up in front of everybody and told Ulfar why. The well is below the byre, he said. It was the water. He was sorry, the boy whispers. He was crying. But he would not stop saying it.

"Ulfar thought he was being told his well was cursed. And that Unkel had known." The boy opens his own hand in the red light and draws a finger across the palm, where the knife went. "Hrapp took it off him. So now Hrapp has to be angry with his brother and grateful to his brother's enemy, both together. He is not made for it."[else]Nobody tells you. It has been lying about in plain sight all day, and the pieces come together as the hall's stories about you came together last night.

There is a place on the bench beside Hrapp where nobody ever sits. There is a farm one bend up the water that Kol's errands never seem to pass. Behind that farm, on the slope, in the last of the light before supper, there was a small new mound with white stones set round it. And below the byre there was a well, with a hurdle laid across its mouth and a rock on top of the hurdle.

"Who shut the well?" you ask Kol, in the dark.

"Ulfar." His whisper comes from somewhere near your shoulder. "After Unkel told him it had killed his boy. He told him in here, in front of everyone. He was crying." A pause, while Kol turns it over. "Ulfar cut him. Hrapp is Ulfar's brother, and it was Hrapp who stopped it. That is why Hrapp does the voice. He has to do something."[/if]

He was right about the well. Anybody from your side of the stone would have said the same. The fire sinks, and a dog turns round three times in the straw and lies down, and nobody in the hall is asleep.

n_stone.title: The white stone
n_stone.text:
You climb the hill with Kol in the grey before sunrise, while the hall is still a dark shape breathing smoke. The moss is easier going up. Below, the fjord is filling slowly with light from the far end, like a bowl being filled with milk.

At the boulder Kol puts his face to the seam of quartz, breathes in, and beckons. It is still there, for anybody who comes close enough for the wet stone to touch their nose: woodsmoke, and low tide, and under them, thin as a thread, the hot dusty smell of the heater in your uncle's shed. Yesterday it reached as far as the path. When Unkel first came, Kol says, it was strong enough to fetch the dog up from the yard. It has come and gone ever since, like the water in the fjord, only far slower. He has been watching it for a year, in case it turned out to matter.

"It goes somewhere." He is not asking. "He went in there. I saw his back go in, and then the stone was only a stone." His small hand is spread flat on the quartz, covering the nine marks. "Where does it go?"

choices.text: Tell him it goes to a country a very long way off.
choices.text_after:
"A country a long way off," you say. "Further than the ships go."

"Further than the empty land?"

"A good deal further."

He is quiet for a time. The edge of the world, for him, has always been somewhere just past the islands, and now he is picking it up and carrying it further off. "Then the smell is that country," he says. He leans in and fills his chest with the air of your uncle's heater, and lets it out again, satisfied. Before you are back in the yard three people have been told that the white stone goes to the country beyond the empty land. One of them sets off up the hill at once, to smell it.

choices.text: Tell him the truth.
choices.text_after:
"It goes to this same hill," you say. "A very long time from now. More winters than you could count if you counted all your life. There's no hall. There's a road."

He does not laugh. He turns and looks down at the hall, at the smoke lying along the grass of its roof, and the two boats on the shingle, and a woman crossing the yard with a pail, and he goes on looking.

"Is it still called this?" he says. The name of the place, when he tells it to you, is three plain words: the bay, and the farm, and the man who first cleared it. "Will you look? When you are there. Whether it is still called this."

You tell him you will. His hand is still on the stone.

choices.text: Tell him you will tell him when he is older.
choices.text_after:
"I'll tell you when you're older," you say.

He gives you the look that every child of eleven has given every adult who ever said it, in any year at all. "Unkel said that," he says. "He said it about the stone, and the beasts in the water, and why the moon follows you home. I am already older than I was when he said it."

He takes his hand off the stone, whistles up the dog, and starts down the hill ahead of you. He does not ask again. Halfway down he stops and looks back at the boulder with one eye narrowed, exactly as Finn looks along a plank.

n_surety.title: What you leave
n_surety.text:
Thorgrim is standing in the middle of the yard when you come down, with his thumbs in his belt and Aud at his shoulder, and a great many people have found something that needs doing within earshot.

"Orm says the weather turns tomorrow," he says. "Kol says the stone is closing. And I say that the last one of you who went up that hill took half a pound of my silver with him." He does not sound angry. He sounds like a man who lay awake over it, and had it in an order before morning. "You may go and look for him. I would sooner he were found than not. But you will leave me something, so that I know you mean to come back down."

choices.text: Leave him what you carried.
choices.text_after:
[if kit == bag]The bag goes down on the packed earth in front of him, and its weight leaves your shoulder. Everything you know how to do is in it. Thorgrim looks at it without touching it. "That is a real thing," he says. "Unkel would not have left his." Aud carries it into the hall herself, to the far end where the locked chests are, and a key turns.[elif kit == notebook]You hold out the notebook. Thorgrim takes it in both hands, opens it, and studies a page of your uncle's capitals for some time, gravely, upside down. "This is his," he says. "All of what he knew?"

"All of what he wrote down."

He passes it to Aud. It goes into the purse at her belt, and her hand rests on the flap a moment longer than it needs to.[else]There is little enough left in the sack: the end of the sugar, two cards of needles, the tin of pepper. Thorgrim weighs it in one hand. Then he draws out a single card of needles, tucks it into his belt, and holds the rest out to you again. "Nobody should start a journey with nothing to give," he says. "Unkel taught me that. He taught me by doing it."[/if]

choices.text: Give him your oath.
choices.text_after:
"I'll swear to it," you say.

The yard goes quiet. Somebody is sent running, and comes back from the high seat with a ring of iron as thick as a thumb, dark and smooth with handling. It is cold, and heavier than it looks. Thorgrim shows you where to lay your hand. He speaks the words a few at a time, and you give them back to him half a beat late, through the brass ear, as you have given back everything since the hill: to come down that hill again, with your kinsman, or with what he owes.

When it is done nobody smiles, and nobody speaks. A hen walks across the silence. The ring is carried back into the hall.

choices.text: Ask whoever you worked beside to speak for you.
choices.text_after:
[if road.day == boat]Finn says it before you can ask. "{He} held the right end," he says. "I will stand for {him}." His father looks at him as if he had put a plank on upside down.[elif road.day == bench]It is Hild who steps out, with the stick in her hand. "I will stand for {him}," she says. Gyda makes a noise. "{He} will come back," Hild says, "because I have not finished asking."[else]Nobody is more surprised than Hrapp. "I owe {him} a breath," he says, to the ground. "I will stand for {him}. If {he} does not come back I am quit of it, and if {he} does I am quit of it, and either way I would like it to be over."

It is the least gracious surety anybody in the yard has ever heard, and Thorgrim takes it at once.[/if]

n_goodbye.title: The yard
n_goodbye.text:
They will not hear of your going before the noon meal, and so it is under a high pale sun that you cross the yard for the last time, with the smell of the cooking fire in your clothes.

[if road.day == boat]Finn walks beside you as far as the edge of the stubble. He has something in his fist, and at the last moment he opens it: a rivet, one of the clenched iron ones from the fifth plank, still bright where the hammer flattened it. "It is the one beside your hole," he says, looking at the fjord. "It would have wanted replacing anyway. Bring it back, and I will put it in the ship."[elif road.day == bench]Hild walks beside you as far as the edge of the stubble. From her belt she takes a second stick, the length of a hand, new-cut and white, without a mark on it. "One edge for what you see that works," she says. "One edge for what does not. I want to know whether it is the same there." She does not say where there is. She puts the stick in your hand and folds her arms.[else]The boy from the bellows walks beside you as far as the edge of the stubble, because Hrapp would not be seen to. He opens his fist. In it is a nail: square, new-drawn, with the blue of the fire still on it, the first thing to come out of the forge since the bellows were mended. "He says it is not a gift," the boy says. "He said I was to say that."[/if]

Aud is standing in the doorway of the hall with her sleeves pushed back to the elbow. She does not come down. But when you look round from the edge of the field she lifts one hand, and in it, pale against the dark of the door, is the horn spoon. She holds it up long enough to be seen. Then she goes in.

choices.text: Go up the hill.

e_door.title: The door
e_door.text:
Kol comes with you as far as the boulder, and stops, and takes hold of the dog by the scruff.

The smell is almost gone. But there is a place on the quartz, under the nine marks, where the rain is not landing. The stone there is dry, and the air close to it is warm against your hand. It does not smell of the shed any longer. It smells sweeter than that: wet cedar, and charcoal burning somewhere near. Half hidden under the moss, stuck to the rock, is a strip of masking tape that was not there three days ago.

::clue next_label::

Below you the hall lies where it lay on the first afternoon, with the smoke spread flat along the grass of its roof. The keel shows as a pale line in the mouth of the boat shed. The two boats are on the shingle. Down in the yard somebody carrying two buckets has stopped, and is shading her eyes. Kol has let go of the dog and is waving with both arms above his head, as a boy waves at a ship.

The quartz is warm under your palm. Nine times he stood here, with his hand flat on this stone. Then the hill is gone.

p_shed.title: The shed
p_shed.text:
The letter comes by post, because your uncle Walter has never trusted a telephone. It is a single sheet folded in three, and the block capitals are pressed so hard into the paper that they can be read with a thumb from the back.

::clue letter::

Every letter he has ever sent you ends with that last line. He has been writing it since you were nine years old, on birthday cards and Christmas cards and once on a postcard from a tractor show, and the Christmas cards are addressed to her. Nobody else gets letters from him at all. He does not say which Saturday, and so the first one goes by with the page lying on the kitchen counter under the car keys, and it is the Saturday after that when the truck finally turns off the highway onto his road.

Two hours of gravel follow, with the dust standing up behind and the fields gone to stubble on either side. His yard light is burning at noon. His own truck sits where it always sits, leaning a little on the flat tire that was pointed out to him in April, and the big door of the machine shed has been rolled back exactly one foot, which is the width of the cat.

Inside it is warm, and smells of diesel and cold coffee. A heater ticks away in the corner with nobody near it. On the workbench stands a mug with a skin on it, and beside the mug a radio turned down low, where a man with a patient voice is reading out the price of canola to an empty room.
[break]
In the middle of the floor, bolted to the concrete, stands a door frame. There is no door in it and no wall on either side of it, only seven feet of square steel tube with the light from the windows falling straight through. Cables as thick as a wrist trail from its feet to a rack of equipment against the wall. Most of what is on the rack could be anything. One piece of it is the arc welder that vanished from your mother's garage four years ago, on an afternoon when he drove over specially to help look for it.

[if occupation == welder]The welds catch your eye before anything else does, as welds always will. Every joint on the frame has been ground flat and brushed over with thick grey paint, and under the paint the bead still shows in lumps, like something buried in a hurry. A whole summer in your shop went into teaching him to lay a clean one. This is what he kept of it, and it is holding up whatever this thing is.[elif occupation == nurse]It is the bench that catches your eye, as a mess on a ward always does before the patient. A roll of gauze lies there with its wrapper torn open by teeth. Beside it stands a bottle of the brown antiseptic that nobody has stocked since your training, and a tea towel gone stiff and dark along one edge. Somebody dressed a cut here with one hand, fast, and did it about as well as your uncle does anything.[elif occupation == teacher]It is the shelf above the bench that catches your eye, as shelves always do. The Old Norse grammar is there, the one that left your house two Christmases ago and never came back, with its spine cracked open at the verbs. A road atlas of Italy leans against it. Next to that is a paperback history of Japan, with a bus ticket marking a place a third of the way through. Your uncle has never been known to finish a book. Here are three he has started.[else]It is the power supply that catches your eye, since somebody's ought to. The cables run back along the floor to the panel by the door, where the breaker for the grain dryer has been pulled out and something home-made of copper bar bolted in its place. On the wall above it, burned into the plywood, is a scorch mark in the shape of a spread hand. Nothing in this building was made to carry what that frame draws, and the building has said so.[/if]

Half a sheet of paper lies under a wrench on the bench, torn across the bottom.

::clue note::

The thumbprint beside his initial is brown and dry, and has cracked a little where the paper was bent. Coffee does not dry that colour.
[break]
Next to the note sits a small case lined with grey foam, cut to hold two of something. One hollow is empty. In the other lies a curl of brass no bigger than a hearing aid, with a hook to go over the ear, and across the lid of the case he has stuck a strip of masking tape.

::clue ear_label::

There is a label very like it on the dashboard of his truck, just above the fuel gauge.

Through the frame the back wall of the shed is plain to see: the pegboard with its painted outlines of tools, the calendar from the co-op turned to the right month. Everything is where it should be. But the air between the uprights is a shade darker than the air on either side, as the air in any doorway is, and a draught is coming through it that lifts the corner of the note on the bench. It smells of woodsmoke, and of low tide. The nearest sea is three days' drive from here.

The cat has made a nest of a horse blanket against the far wall, as far from the frame as it can get and still be out of the rain, and from there it watches without lifting its chin.

A second strip of tape is stuck to the frame itself, at the height of your eyes.

::clue frame_label::

So there is one hand to fill. Your work bag is out in the truck, because he asked for it. His notebook lies on the bench beside the note, black, swollen fat with use, held shut by a rubber band. And above the kettle is a shelf he has labelled TRADE in the same capitals, with a bag of sugar on it, and a tin of pepper, and three cards of steel needles from the fabric shop in town.

choices.text: Fetch your work bag from the truck.
choices.text_after:
The bag is on the passenger seat under a coat, heavy and familiar, and its strap finds the groove it wore in your shoulder years ago.

The brass thing hooks over your ear and sits there warm, as though it had only just come off somebody else's. The note goes into your jacket pocket. Your phone and your lighter are in your jeans already.

Behind you the radio is still murmuring prices. The draught from the frame touches your face, cool and salt, and you step through it as if over a garden hose, with your one hand full.

choices.text_after:
